name: Reading the Results Honestly
title: Reading the Results Honestly
answer: Reading pilot results honestly means treating the numbers with care before deciding to scale a tool. Volunteer teachers, novelty effects, weak comparison points, and hidden gaps between groups can all make a tool look better than it is. The idea matters because a district that misreads a pilot may scale something that does not actually help students.

sections.body: This idea is about how to interpret the results once a pilot has finished, rather than assuming a positive number means the tool works. The problem it solves is that pilots are easy to misread: the teachers who volunteer tend to be strong and enthusiastic, so their classrooms may do well with any new tool. Without a comparison group of similar classrooms, a district cannot separate the tool's effect from the teacher's. Novelty is a second trap, because students often work harder with something new and that boost fades as the tool becomes ordinary. The idea asks leaders to slow down and read the evidence carefully before scaling.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, a school reads pilot results by comparing the pilot classrooms with similar classrooms that did not use the tool, so the tool's effect can be told apart from the teacher's skill. Because a six week pilot can catch a novelty bump and mistake it for a lasting gain, a promising result should be checked again later in the year. The comparison point also matters: a fair pilot compares the new tool with the best current option, not with an empty classroom, since a tool that beats doing nothing may not beat what the school already has. Finally, schools look at who benefited, reporting results separately for students with disabilities, English learners, and students from low income families whenever the numbers are large enough to mean something. The text does not give grade band variations for this idea.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this idea's evidence through two reviews it cites. A review of generative AI studies found that the boost to student motivation shrank the longer a study ran (Liu et al., 2025). One review found that intelligent tutoring systems helped students in general, but that the advantage shrank when they were compared with other practice software rather than with no software at all (Letourneau, 2025). These findings support the book's warnings about novelty and about weak comparison points.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits here are about what a pilot can and cannot show. A pilot without a comparison group cannot separate the tool's effect from the teacher's, and a short pilot can mistake a novelty bump for a lasting gain, so promising results should be checked again later in the year. A tool that only beats doing nothing may not beat what the school already has, so the fair comparison is with the best current option. An average gain can hide a split where some students improved and others fell behind, so results for students with disabilities, English learners, and students from low income families should be reported separately whenever the numbers are large enough to mean something. A tool that widens a gap should not scale, even if the average looks good, and that judgment stays with the people reading the results.
